progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: B4 to B6a: DNA nucleotides with A pairing T and C pairing G by hydrogen bonds; antiparallel strands with 5' and 3' ends; one strand acts as a template; a gene is a section of DNA; eukaryotic DNA is wound on histones in a nucleus with an envelope and is loosened where a gene is read; bacteria have no nucleus. Year 11: enzymes, organelles, the nuclear envelope. Not assumed: RNA, uracil, ribose, mRNA, transcription, RNA polymerase, promoter, template and coding strand as transcription terms, nuclear pore, codon.
progression.startsWith: The DNA stays in the nucleus while the ribosomes that build proteins are outside it, and the question of how the instructions in a gene get from one place to the other.
progression.stopsAfter: Saying why a copy is needed; defining a gene; giving three differences between RNA and DNA; describing how RNA polymerase binds the promoter, separates the strands and builds mRNA by pairing with the template strand (A with U, T with A, C with G, G with C); saying which way each strand runs and why; writing the mRNA for a given template with ends; saying the mRNA matches the coding strand with U for T; describing release, the unchanged gene and export through a nuclear pore; saying why many temporary copies help; contrasting transcription with replication; naming codons as groups of three; predicting that a changed template base changes a codon. It does not say what codons mean. No pre-mRNA processing, transcription factors or polymerase types.
progression.nextLesson: B6c: how a ribosome turns the mRNA code into a chain of amino acids.

teaching.task: Explain how a cell copies one gene into mRNA and why it needs a copy, and write the mRNA for a given strand with its ends.
teaching.causalExplanation: The DNA stays in the nucleus and the ribosomes are outside, so the cell sends out a copy of the gene. RNA polymerase binds the promoter and opens the strands, and it copies only the template strand because the template fixes every base of the mRNA. New nucleotides join only at the 3' end, so the mRNA grows 5' to 3' and, because paired strands run in opposite directions, the template is read 3' to 5'. U pairs with A as T does, so the mRNA matches the coding strand with U for T. The gene re-pairs behind the polymerase and is unchanged; the mRNA leaves through a nuclear pore, and many temporary copies let one gene make a lot of protein, with control by stopping the copying.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on the painted cell and the problem of a gene stuck in the nucleus, explains the copy with a recipe-book analogy and states where it breaks, builds the RNA differences on the molecules, shows one strand and the direction as separate beats, works the site template tile by tile with wrong tiles turned away, checks against the coding strand, then asks two harder unseen items, each followed by a model answer built one point at a time.
teaching.openingDecision: Your DNA never leaves the nucleus, but the machines that build proteins are outside it. How does a gene get out?
teaching.understandingCheck: Given a double strand with ends labelled and the polymerase moving left to right, identify the template strand using the direction rule and write the mRNA with its 5' and 3' ends (top strand 3' TGC AAT CGG 5' is the template; mRNA 5' ACG UUA GCC 3'). Then explain why a toxin that stops RNA polymerase moving along DNA makes a cell produce less and less protein although the DNA and ribosomes are undamaged.
teaching.curriculumScope: Model the process of polypeptide synthesis, including transcription and translation, and assess the importance of mRNA and tRNA (Module 5, ACSBL079). This video owns transcription and the importance of mRNA; translation and tRNA are the next video. Pre-mRNA processing, transcription factors, polymerase types and what each codon means are deferred.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, the painted cell protein synthesis plate and recipe book, and a coded transcription board (nucleus close-up with a dashed envelope arc and a pore, plum DNA ladder, B4 jigsaw base tiles with a new amber U tile, a terracotta mRNA strand, an ochre RNA polymerase bean, end tags and process arrows). The coding strand dims to about 35 per cent while the template is read. Blue and green are not used for mRNA.
design.transitionPlan: The painted cell opens the lesson and the camera zooms into the coded nucleus board; the analogy plate slides in and out; the board persists through scenes 3 to 8 with the polymerase and the dim rule carrying attention; the camera pans to the envelope arc and cuts back out to the painted cell for the export; the board splits once for the replication contrast; each attempt card clears the aids and its feedback follows at once, turning the card into pictures and model-answer lines; the next chip slides in; scene crossfade with settle.
